record.original_question: Given an argumentation framework F, a set C of arguments, and a modification type Phi specifying allowed attack additions or removals, the (sigma,Phi)-characteristic N^F_{sigma,Phi}(C) is 0 if C is already contained in some sigma-extension, is the minimum attack-edit distance needed to make C contained in some sigma-extension when this is possible, and is infinity otherwise. For semi-stable semantics, are there local criteria for determining N^F_{ss,Phi}(C), analogous to known local criteria for stable, preferred, complete, and admissible semantics?

evidence.quote: This value, called (σ, Φ)-characteristic, depends on the underlying semantics σ and type of allowed modifications Φ.
Whereas Nst,Φ and Npr ,Φ are already computable a characterization in case of semi-stable semantics remains an open problem.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
An (abstract) argumentation framework is a pair $F=(A,R)$ where $A$ is a finite set of arguments and $R\subseteq A\times A$ is an attack relation. For a set $S\subseteq A$, write $S^+ = S\cup\{a\in A : \exists b\in S,\,(b,a)\in R\}$. A set $S\subseteq A$ is conflict-free if there are no $a,b\in S$ with $(a,b)\in R$; $S$ is admissible if it is conflict-free and every $a\in S$ is defended by $S$ (i.e. for every $(b,a)\in R$ there is $c\in S$ with $(c,b)\in R$); $S$ is complete if it is admissible and contains every argument it defends; $S$ is a preferred extension if it is a $\subseteq$-maximal complete extension; $S$ is a semi-stable extension (semantics ss) if it is a complete extension whose range $S^+$ is $\subseteq$-maximal among all complete extensions.
 
Let $\Phi$ be one of the following "modification types": (i) only additions of attacks are allowed, (ii) only removals of attacks are allowed, or (iii) arbitrary additions and removals of attacks are allowed (the set of arguments $A$ is never changed). The $\Phi$-edit distance between two frameworks $F=(A,R)$ and $F'=(A,R')$ is the size of the symmetric difference $|R\triangle R'|$ subject to the constraints imposed by $\Phi$.
 
For a semantics $\sigma$, a framework $F=(A,R)$, and a set $C\subseteq A$, define
$$N^{F}_{\sigma,\Phi}(C) \;=\; \begin{cases} 0, & \text{if $C$ is contained in some $\sigma$-extension of $F$,}\\ \min\{|R\triangle R'| : C\subseteq E\text{ for some $\sigma$-extension $E$ of $(A,R')$}\}, & \text{if such an $F'$ exists under $\Phi$,}\\ \infty, & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
 
For the semantics $\sigma\in\{\text{stable, preferred, complete, admissible}\}$, $N^{F}_{\sigma,\Phi}(C)$ admits a "local" characterization, i.e. it can be computed from locally checkable conditions on $F$ and $C$ (for example via value functions depending only on $C$, its attackers, and its defenders).
 
Problem. Provide local criteria that determine $N^{F}_{ss,\Phi}(C)$ for the semi-stable semantics under each of the three modification types $\Phi$; equivalently, exhibit a computable characterization of $N^{F}_{ss,\Phi}(C)$ in terms of locally checkable properties of $F$ and $C$ analogous to those known for stable, preferred, complete, and admissible semantics.
artifact.status_search_result: A characterization of the minimal-change characteristic for stable and preferred semantics is known, but for semi-stable semantics a local-criteria characterization remains unestablished in the literature on enforcement and minimal change in abstract argumentation. No subsequent work was located that explicitly resolves the semi-stable case, so the problem appears to still be open.

status_evidence.title: What Does it Take to Enforce an Argument? Minimal Change in Abstract Argumentation
status_evidence.snippet: For several Dung semantics, this problem can be decided by local criteria encoded by the so-called value functions.
status_evidence.claim: Local criteria (value functions) are known for several Dung semantics, but semi-stable is not among the semantics covered.

status_evidence.title: Computational Complexity of Semi-stable Semantics in Abstract Argumentation Frameworks
status_evidence.snippet: Semi-stable semantics has higher complexity than stable/preferred for several reasoning tasks.
status_evidence.claim: Semi-stable semantics is computationally harder, suggesting why simple local criteria are not immediate.
